catalog_quote: This section deals with the lexical function of tone in Ajumbu. Ajumbu is thus considered as a tone language because in section 3.2.1 that follows, it is shown that tone are distinctive and contribute in the meaning of lexical items. 4.2.1 Inventory of Tones Ajumbu counts thee (03) level and four (04) contour tones as examined in the following subsections. ... 7.3 Note on Ajumbu Tones Ajumbu is a three-level tone language (High, Mid, and Low). Following the principle of Tadadjeu & Sadembouo (1984) which states that when a language has three level tones two are marked and one is left out, the high and low tones will be represented in the Ajumbu alphabet and the mid tone will be left out. Contour tones are going to be derived through orthographic principles.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ajumbu is analysed as a tone language with three underlying level tonemes (H, M, L) and derived contours; the 149-page phonology contains no statement about word stress or accent (no prominence section, no claim that stress exists or is absent). Good et al. 2011 sect. 3.4.2.3 likewise describes only a three-way tone contrast.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the only length-related remark (Good et al. 2011: 135) is that first-syllable vowels of verbs are relatively long, treated as a possible length contrast or verb marker, not as stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone on roots (CV, CVC noun/verb roots; V, N, CV pronouns); no word- or phrase-level stress domain described.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the single-village language Ajumbu (a.k.a. Mbu', formerly listed as Mbuk in Hamm et al. 2002), ISO muc = Glottolog mbuu1238; not to be confused with Mbuk (mbuk1244) of the Bum area. Woungly's data: own fieldwork plus KPAAM-CAM corpora (Tschonghongei 2019 wordlist).

sources.note: Nothing. Full phonology (27 C, 11 V, 3 level tonemes H/M/L + 4 surface contours, syllable types, tone patterns on noun/verb roots, tone processes, orthography); 'Ajumbu is thus considered as a tone language' (p.63) and 'Ajumbu is a three-level tone language (High, Mid, and Low)' (sect. 7.3, p.109). The words stress/accent occur only in generic lit-review sentences about lenition/devocalization (pp.20-21), never about Ajumbu. No prominence/accent section.
